problemText: Earth's lithosphere is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. Which of the following correctly identifies what lies directly beneath these plates?
choices: The outer core, which is made of solid iron and nickel
A layer of liquid magma that covers the entire area under all the plates
The asthenosphere, a layer of solid rock in the mantle that flows extremely slowly
The crust, which is the same rigid layer as the plates themselves
hints: Think about the structure of Earth's layers going from the surface downward.
Remember that the asthenosphere is solid rock, not liquid, even though it can flow over very long time periods.

problemText: A piece of oceanic crust sits on top of a tectonic plate. A piece of continental crust sits on top of a different tectonic plate. A geologist observes that these two pieces of crust move together as one connected unit, even though one is continental and one is oceanic. Which explanation best fits this observation?
choices: Continental and oceanic crust are attracted to each other by magnetic forces that pull them together
The mantle below them causes each piece to move independently, but they happen to move in the same direction by chance
The continental crust drags the oceanic crust along because it is denser and heavier
Both pieces of crust are part of the same single tectonic plate, a connected slab of lithosphere, so they move together
hints: What is the definition of a tectonic plate? What does it include?
A plate is not just one type of crust — it is a single connected slab of lithosphere that can carry different kinds of crust together.

problemText: Scientists measure the position of two ocean-floor plates on either side of a long underwater ridge. Each year, the gap between these plates grows wider by 6 centimeters. After 1 million years, approximately how much wider will the gap be compared to today?
choices: Approximately 600 kilometers wider
Approximately 60 kilometers wider
Approximately 6,000 kilometers wider
Approximately 60,000 kilometers wider
hints: Start by converting 1 million years into a regular number so you can multiply it by the yearly rate.
After you multiply centimeters per year by the number of years, remember to convert centimeters to kilometers by dividing by 100,000.

problemText: Two neighboring tectonic plates are drifting apart at a rate of 2 centimeters per year. A student claims that because this movement is so slow, mantle convection cannot be powerful enough to move entire plates. Which statement best evaluates this claim?
choices: The claim is correct because 2 centimeters per year is a negligibly small amount, so mantle convection must be too weak to do real work
The claim is incorrect because even tiny yearly movements add up to large distances over millions of years, which is the time scale over which mantle convection actually operates
The claim is incorrect because plate motion is measured relative to the asthenosphere below them, not relative to human timescales, so slow yearly motion still reflects powerful mantle forces
The claim is correct because mantle convection only happens in the crust, not in the deeper layers that are needed to move lithospheric plates
hints: Think about the time scale that mantle convection works on. Does it operate over days, years, or millions of years?
A small number multiplied by an enormous number of years can produce a very large total distance.

problemText: A geologist finds a coastline where the continent meets the ocean. The student's first thought is that this coastline marks the edge of a tectonic plate. However, the geologist measures the motion of rocks on both sides of the coastline and finds that the continent and the neighboring ocean floor move together in the same direction. Explain why this measurement contradicts the student's first idea about where the plate boundary is located.
choices: The coastline cannot be a plate boundary because plate boundaries are defined by the edges of connected pieces of crust, and coastlines mark where land and water meet, which are different definitions of the same location
The coastline is a plate boundary, but the ocean floor next to it is floating on liquid magma instead of moving with the plate as a solid unit
If the continent and ocean floor move together as one unit, they must be part of the same single plate, so the plate boundary is not at the coastline but somewhere farther out in the ocean
The plate boundary is at the coastline, but the continent and ocean floor only appear to move together because they are both sitting on top of the same mantle convection cell
hints: What is a tectonic plate? Is it defined by where dry land ends and ocean water begins, or by something else?
If two pieces of crust move together as one connected unit, what does that tell you about whether they are part of the same plate?

problemText: A student reads that the Pacific Plate moves at an average rate of 10 centimeters per year, while the North American Plate moves at an average rate of 2 centimeters per year. The student then learns that mantle convection is a single, slow, circulating pattern of solid rock moving through the deep mantle. Based on these facts, what is the most reasonable conclusion about why different plates move at different speeds?
choices: Different plates move at different speeds because they are made of different materials — some plate rock is denser and heavier than other plate rock, causing variations in how fast they can be pushed or pulled across the asthenosphere

Different plates move at different speeds because some plates are pushed by mantle convection while others are pulled by gravity at subduction zones, creating two separate driving mechanisms that produce different velocity results

Different plates move at different speeds because larger plates experience greater friction with the asthenosphere below them, which reduces their velocity compared to smaller plates that experience less resistance

Different plates move at different speeds because the asthenosphere under each plate flows at a different rate in its local region, even though all parts of it are part of the same global convection pattern
hints: Mantle convection is one global pattern of motion, but does every part of that pattern move at the same speed?
The asthenosphere is the layer the plates ride on. If different regions of the asthenosphere in the pattern are flowing at different speeds, how would that affect the plates above them?

problemText: Alfred Wegener proposed that all Earth's continents were once joined together in a single landmass. What did he call this ancient supercontinent?
choices: Gondwana
Pangaea
Laurasia
Atlantis
hints: This is the specific name Wegener gave to the joined landmass in 1912.
The word combines Greek roots meaning 'all' and 'earth.'

problemText: A scientist studying two continents separated by an ocean notices that a distinctive sequence of rock layers—the same types of rock in the same order, all of the same age—is found in both locations. What does this matching rock-layer sequence suggest about the continents' past?
choices: Ocean currents carried identical rock material from one continent to the other over millions of years.
The continents formed at the same time in different locations and have always been separated by an ocean.
The two continents were once connected or positioned side by side, and have since moved apart.
The rock layers formed underwater on the seafloor and then rose above the ocean to create the continents.
hints: Consider what a rock layer records about the conditions present when it formed.
If the same sequence is now separated by an ocean, what does that tell you about where those rock sequences were when they formed?

problemText: Glossopteris was a seed fern whose seeds were too heavy to be carried far by wind. Yet fossils of Glossopteris are found on South America, southern Africa, India, Australia, and Antarctica—continents that today are separated by oceans. Why is the presence of Glossopteris on all these continents considered evidence for continental drift?
choices: Because ocean currents were strong enough in the past to carry heavy seeds across vast distances of open ocean between continents.
Because Glossopteris seeds had special air-filled structures and waxy coatings that allowed them to float and survive drifting across salt water for long periods.
Because Glossopteris evolved separately on each continent at different times through natural selection, which proves those continents were isolated from one another.
Because the seeds were too heavy to drift on the wind across oceans, the continents must have been joined or very close together when Glossopteris lived.
hints: Think about what the organism could and could not do on its own.
If something cannot reach a place by itself, what must be true about the geography when it was alive?

problemText: Mesosaurus was a small reptile that lived only in fresh water and could not survive or swim across salty ocean water. Its fossils appear in matching-age rock layers in both South America and southern Africa. At the same time, scientists have found matching sequences of rock layers in the same regions, and the coastlines of these two continents fit together like puzzle pieces. How do these three independent kinds of evidence work together to support continental drift?
choices: Each type of evidence separately suggests the continents were once joined; when all three point to the same conclusion, the case becomes much stronger.
The Mesosaurus fossils alone are sufficient proof of continental drift, because an organism that cannot cross salt water could not have reached both continents by any other means.
The matching rock layers prove the continents drifted apart, but Mesosaurus fossils and coastline shape are unreliable indicators because they depend on other factors besides continental movement.
The fossil and rock evidence measure different things but both support the same idea, so including coastline information creates redundancy rather than strengthening the case.
hints: When different types of clues—a fossil, a rock sequence, and a coastline shape—all agree on the same answer, how does that change the strength of the conclusion?
Consider why it matters that the evidence comes from living things, non-living rock, and geography, rather than just one category.

problemText: Scientists mapping the Atlantic Ocean floor discovered a mirror-image pattern of magnetic stripes in the rock on either side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Rock at the same distance from the ridge on both sides shows the same magnetic direction and is the same age. Why did this seafloor magnetic-stripe evidence succeed in convincing most scientists that continents move, when Wegener's earlier evidence of matching coastlines, fossils, and rock layers had been widely rejected for decades?
choices: Magnetic stripes are stronger evidence than fossils because scientists can measure the magnetic direction and age of rock more precisely using modern laboratory instruments and methods.
The magnetic stripe pattern showed direct, measurable evidence that the ocean floor itself is being created and moving outward from the ridge, something Wegener's evidence could not demonstrate.
The magnetic stripes proved that Wegener's fossil and rock evidence was inaccurate, showing that the continents had never actually moved from their original positions.
The magnetic stripes were discovered using technology that did not exist during Wegener's time, which explained why his earlier evidence had been rejected by the scientific community.
hints: Wegener's evidence showed continents once fit together, but what crucial piece of information was still missing that made scientists doubt the idea?
What is different about magnetic stripe evidence—what can it show that coastlines, fossils, and rock layers could not show?

problemText: A geologist finds that a small, freshwater reptile is preserved in matching-age rock on Continent X and Continent Y, which are now separated by a wide, salty ocean. The same rock layers that contain the reptile's fossils are also found in both locations, in the same sequence and age. However, when the geologist checks whether a living species of this reptile could survive a long ocean crossing, experiments show it can survive in salt water for extended periods. How should this new information about the reptile's salt-water tolerance affect the interpretation of this fossil evidence for continental drift?
choices: The fossil evidence now proves the continents never moved, because the reptile's demonstrated ability to survive salt water means it could have traveled across the ocean independently.
The matching rock layers lose their power as evidence once we learn the reptile could tolerate salt water and therefore could have crossed the ocean on its own by swimming.

The fossil evidence no longer strongly supports continental drift for this particular organism, because the reptile could have crossed the ocean on its own; other independent evidence like the matching rock sequences remains valid.
The salt-water tolerance must have developed after the continents separated, which actually strengthens the case that the continents were originally connected together in the past.
hints: Remember that fossil evidence for continental drift depends on a specific property of the organism—what property makes it work?
If the organism could have crossed the ocean under its own power, can that fossil alone still be used as evidence? What other evidence in this scenario can still stand on its own?

problemText: Which of the following landforms is built when two plates carrying continental crust push directly into each other and neither plate sinks beneath the other?
choices: Fold mountains
Ocean trench
Mid-ocean ridge
Volcanic island arc
hints: Think about what happens to rock when two plates squeeze together but cannot sink.
Continental crust has similar density on both sides, so one plate cannot dive beneath the other.

problemText: At a plate boundary, one plate made of dense oceanic crust is bending downward and sinking beneath another oceanic plate. As the sinking plate goes deeper, melted rock rises through the plate above it and erupts at the ocean floor. What two landforms are being built side by side at this boundary?
choices: A mid-ocean ridge and a rift valley
An ocean trench and a volcanic island arc
Fold mountains and a rift valley
Two mid-ocean ridges pulling apart
hints: Look for clues that tell you plates are squeezing together, not pulling apart.
The melted rock rising and erupting tells you volcanoes are forming, and the sinking plate creates a deep valley.

problemText: Two ocean-floor plates are moving away from each other along a divergent boundary. Magma fills the widening gap between them and hardens into new rock. This process is happening all along the boundary as the plates continue to pull apart. What landform is forming at this boundary?
choices: A rift valley with raised sides
An ocean trench
A mid-ocean ridge
Fold mountains
hints: The key is that the plates are pulling apart, not squeezing together.
New rock is hardening from magma along the crack where the plates are separating.

problemText: Two plates made of continental crust are slowly pulling apart from each other. The land between them is stretching thinner and dropping lower than the ground on either side. Eventually, if the plates continue to pull apart for millions of years, ocean water could cover the low ground between them. Based on the current state and the likely future result, name both the landform being built now and what type of plate boundary is causing it.
choices: An ocean trench at a convergent boundary; if subduction continues, the trench will deepen further
Fold mountains at a convergent boundary; if compression continues, the mountains will rise higher
A mid-ocean ridge at a divergent boundary; if pulling continues, the ridge will grow taller
A rift valley at a divergent boundary; if it widens long enough, it could become a seaway like the Red Sea
hints: Identify first whether the plates are pushing together or pulling apart, then match the crust type to the landform.
Remember that continental crust pulling apart creates a dropped valley with cracked sides, and that this feature can eventually hold ocean water if it keeps widening.

problemText: A geologist finds that at a plate boundary, one plate is bending sharply downward and sinking beneath the other. The plate riding on top is made of continental crust, and it is sitting above the subduction zone. Based on what you know about subduction and how rock behaves when plates collide, which of the following best explains what landforms are most likely to form at this boundary?
choices: A volcanic island arc on land and an ocean trench alongside it, because melted rock rises through the continental plate above
Fold mountains, because continental crust from both plates is crumpling and folding upward as they collide and compress together at a convergent boundary
A mid-ocean ridge, because new oceanic crust is continuously created as magma rises and the two plates move away from each other in opposite directions
A rift valley, because the continental crust is being stretched horizontally and pulled apart by tensional forces at a divergent plate boundary
hints: One plate is sinking (subducting), which means this is a convergent boundary, not a divergent one.
When the sinking plate melts, that melted rock has to go somewhere—it rises through the plate above and erupts, building volcanoes on the overlying continental crust.

problemText: Two plates meet at a boundary. Plate A carries oceanic crust with a density of 3.0 g/cm³. Plate B carries continental crust with a density of 2.7 g/cm³. The two plates are being pushed directly toward each other. Using what you know about density, subduction, and plate-boundary landforms, predict both the direction the plates will move (which one sinks) and the pair of landforms that should form at this boundary. Explain your reasoning using the relationship between crust density and subduction.
choices: Plate B sinks; a mid-ocean ridge and rift valley form because both plates are being pulled apart and new ocean floor is created as magma rises between them
Plate A sinks; an ocean trench and volcanic island arc form because oceanic crust is denser and bends downward, with volcanoes building on Plate B above
Plate B sinks; fold mountains form because continental crust is less dense and rides on top of the sinking oceanic crust, causing both plates to fold and crumple upward
Plate A sinks; fold mountains form because the denser oceanic plate buckles downward and forces the continental crust above it to crumple into a mountain range
hints: Compare the two densities to determine which plate is denser and therefore will subduct.
Remember that when oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, melted rock rises through the continental plate and builds volcanoes on land, along with a trench at the subduction zone.

problemText: At a plate boundary, two large sections of Earth's crust are moving directly away from each other, and the gap between them keeps growing wider. Based only on the direction of motion, what type of plate boundary is this?
choices: Convergent, because the gap is growing wider
Convergent, because the plates are separating from each other
Transform, because the distance between them is changing
Divergent, because the two plates are pulling apart
hints: Ask yourself: which way are the two plates moving relative to each other — apart, together, or sliding past?
The word divergent means the plates are spreading or opening up from each other.

problemText: A scientist measures the positions of two markers placed on opposite sides of a plate boundary, one on each plate. Over a five-year period, the west marker moves 15 kilometers to the west, and the east marker moves 15 kilometers to the east. What type of boundary is this, based solely on the relative motion?
choices: Divergent, because each marker is moving away from the boundary and the space between them is growing
Convergent, because the plates are moving in opposite compass directions relative to each other at the boundary
Transform, because the markers are moving in opposite compass directions and creating friction between plates
Convergent, because the two markers started in contact and their separation proves plates are colliding
hints: Track what is happening to the distance across the boundary — is it growing, shrinking, or staying the same?
The key is not which compass direction each plate moves, but whether the gap between the two plates is opening or closing.

problemText: The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous plate boundary where the Pacific plate and the North American plate grind past each other along a north-south line. Over many years, the land west of the fault has shifted steadily north, while the land east of the fault has shifted steadily south. Measurements show the distance straight across the fault, from west to east, has remained nearly constant. What type of boundary is the San Andreas Fault?
choices: Convergent, because the plates are moving in opposite directions along the boundary line, which indicates they are colliding head-on
Transform, because the two plates are sliding past each other while the distance across the boundary stays about the same
Divergent, because the plate motions are in different compass directions, indicating the plates are separating and spreading apart
Convergent, because the constant distance across the boundary shows the plates are locked together and being compressed
hints: Focus on the distance measured straight across the boundary from one side to the other — is that gap shrinking, growing, or constant?
Different compass directions of motion along a boundary is not the same as plates moving toward or away from each other across the boundary.

problemText: At the boundary beneath the Andes Mountains, one plate carrying open ocean floor is moving steadily toward a neighboring plate that carries a continent. The distance between these two plates has been shrinking for millions of years. A student claims this boundary is not convergent because one side is carrying ocean floor and the other is carrying a continent, not two continents crashing together. Explain whether the student is correct, using only the definition of convergent boundary.
choices: The student is correct; the boundary is actually divergent because one side has ocean floor and the other has a continent, so they cannot move toward each other
The student is correct; a convergent boundary requires two continents colliding together, so a boundary between ocean floor and continental crust cannot be convergent
The student is incorrect; a convergent boundary is defined by the two plates moving toward each other and closing the gap, regardless of whether either plate carries a continent
The student is incorrect; the boundary is transform because ocean floor and continental crust slide horizontally past each other instead of colliding
hints: What is the actual definition of convergent — does it mention continents, or does it describe the relative motion of the plates?
A plate can carry both ocean floor and a continent at the same time; what matters for naming the boundary type is the direction the plates move, not what material they carry.

problemText: Two surveyors measure a plate boundary at different times. In Year 1, the distance across the boundary measured 100 kilometers. In Year 10, that same distance measured 95 kilometers. After Year 10, surveyors discovered that the two sides were sliding past each other along the boundary line, not moving toward it. Based on both the measured distance change and the sliding motion, determine the boundary type and explain why the boundary cannot be transform.
choices: Convergent, because one boundary can only be one type, and the shrinking distance proves it is closing even though sliding also occurs
Transform, because the plates are sliding past each other along the boundary line, which is the defining characteristic of transform motion
Divergent, because the distance decreased from 100 to 95 kilometers, indicating the plates are being pulled apart and creating new space
Convergent, because the distance across the boundary has been shrinking, even though the plates also have a sliding component to their motion
hints: The key question for any boundary type is the distance across the boundary — is it growing, shrinking, or staying constant?
A transform boundary is defined by the distance across it staying about the same; if that distance is actually shrinking, the boundary must be closing, not sliding.

problemText: A geologist studying a plate boundary finds the following data: on one side of the boundary, rock and sediment are moving steadily northeast at an average rate. On the other side, rock and sediment are moving steadily southwest. A student concludes the boundary must be convergent because the two sides are moving toward each other. A second student argues the boundary might not be convergent and suggests checking one more measurement before deciding. What single measurement would help determine whether this boundary is truly convergent, divergent, or transform, and why would that measurement be the deciding factor?
choices: Measure the distance across the boundary perpendicular to the motion directions; if it is shrinking, the boundary is convergent; if it is growing, divergent; if it is staying constant, transform
Measure the speed of each plate separately; the plate moving faster determines whether the boundary is convergent or divergent based on relative velocity
Count how many earthquakes occur per year and measure how deep they are; more deep earthquakes indicate a convergent boundary with subduction occurring
Measure how much new ocean floor or mountain range is being built at the boundary; the amount of new crust created shows whether the boundary is actively converging
hints: Recall that different compass directions of motion at a boundary does not automatically mean the plates are closing in on each other — the gap across the boundary is what actually decides.
The trap in this problem is that northeast and southwest look like opposing directions, but you need to check whether the distance measured perpendicular to the boundary is actually changing.
